summary:
Blinking Sky is an open-source citizen-science tool that lets anyone explore real images from NASA’s SPHEREx mission—and vote on what they see.

Enter an object name or sky coordinates, then blink across dates to spot motion, or across infrared colours to reveal spectral features. Watch an asteroid cross the stars, follow a nearby brown dwarf between observations, or explore the methane absorption characteristic of cold atmospheres. A spectrum builds as the images arrive.
Everything runs in your browser, with no installation or account. Explore a 3D map from the Solar System to distant galaxies, and compare SPHEREx with aligned WISE and optical images.

Combining WISE-selected targets with SPHEREx measurements, we identified 12 cold brown dwarf candidates for which we found no published classification. Their nature remains to be confirmed.

Inspired by Backyard Worlds: Planet 9, a queue of 382 sources invites everyone to contribute. Inspect the images, submit your classification, and compare it with community votes. Blinking Sky turns public space data into an investigation anyone can join.
details:
What does it do?

SPHEREx re-observes the whole sky every six months, in 102 bands of near-infrared light, and no one person can sift through a billion sources alone. Blinking Sky lets anyone watch the sky change in real SPHEREx images, on three time scales: hours for the Solar System, months and years for our nearest neighbours, and no change at all for distant galaxies, which is the reference. It has three parts.
1. A blink viewer. For any object name, or any position typed as coordinates, the visitor blinks between dates to see what moves, and between two colours (4 µm and the methane band at 3.15–3.50 µm) to see what the object is made of. The same exposures give a spectrum of the position, drawn as they arrive.
2. A map with real distances: the Sun, the Earth, the planets and 7,083 asteroids and comets placed where they were on the day SPHEREx saw them; 15,739 ultracool dwarfs already typed by SPHEREx; 43,463 galaxies. Clicking any dot opens its real images.
3. A review queue of 382 red, moving WISE sources for which we found no SPHEREx examination. The visitor looks at one, says what they see, then sees the measurement and what other visitors said. A "Community votes" panel shows the totals and the latest votes.


Try it in one minute at https://blinking-sky.vercel.app (“Open the sky”). Source code: https://github.com/Paulhb7/blinking-sky

- Type “Ceres” in the search box: six real exposures a few hours apart. The stars stay, Ceres moves.

- Open “WISE 0855−0714” and blink “Across dates”: the coldest known brown dwarf, 7 light-years away, shifts between May 2025 and May 2026.

- Open a source under “Candidates · no publication found” and blink “Across colours”: it is there at 4 µm and gone in the methane band.

Tested on the challenge targets
- Barnard’s Star: two exposures, 2025-08-21 and 2026-08-18, near 1.9 µm. Against 18 reference stars, the star shifts north by 10.3–10.6″; Gaia DR3 and the parallax predict 10.3″. The core is saturated.
- WISE 0855−0714: the shift between May 2025 and May 2026 is visible in one blink; the colour blink shows the methane dip.

- Epsilon Indi B: the brown dwarf pair shifts by about one SPHEREx pixel to the south-east between April 2025 and September 2026; "What changed" shows where it was and where it is.

- RW Aurigae: it fades from 2.19 Jy in September 2025 to 1.19 Jy in September 2026 at 3.8–5 µm, 1.8 times fainter, read date by date (quick look).

Links to open them:

- Epsilon Indi B: https://blinking-sky.vercel.app/?ra=331.0960&dec=-56.8010

- RW Aurigae: https://blinking-sky.vercel.app/?ra=76.95642&dec=30.40142

- R Draconis: https://blinking-sky.vercel.app/?ra=248.16758&dec=66.75494

How does it work?

SPHEREx level-2 images are public in a cloud archive that accepts partial requests from a web page. For each exposure, the browser requests the header with the astrometric solution, the wavelength table, and the image rows containing the position—about 0.3 MB instead of a 65 MB file. An index of 1.6 million images, divided into small sky tiles, identifies the exposures covering each position. Each cutout has its background removed and is reprojected onto a common, north-up grid. Exposures within each survey pass are averaged after rejecting single-exposure outliers. No synthetic sources are added, and missing pixels remain black.

To say what an object is, we use one simple test, the methane index: the flux at 3.15–3.50 µm divided by the flux at 3.83–4.20 µm. Below 0.30, with a signal-to-noise ratio of at least 5, we call it a methane dip. On controls, 19 of 21 confirmed cold dwarfs show the dip (the two others have a background star in the pixel), and none of 256 negative controls does. We checked the in-browser reader against a reference analysis in Python: pixel positions agree to a millionth of a pixel.

What benefits does it have?

Anyone can look at real SPHEREx images within seconds, at any position, with no account and nothing to install. Applied to red, moving sources from CatWISE2020, the methane test selects 48 sources consistent with late-T or Y brown dwarfs. Three have published spectroscopic classifications and were recovered without using those classifications in the selection. Another 33 are previously published candidates, for which SPHEREx provides additional spectral evidence. For the remaining 12, we found no published classification in the catalogs and literature searched. These 45 candidates require confirmation, and some of the 12 may already be under investigation by other teams.

The candidate table gives observers a short list for follow-up spectroscopy; it will be deposited on Zenodo after the hackathon. The site is static and reads NASA’s archive directly, so it costs nothing to keep online.

What is the intended impact?

SPHEREx re-observes the whole sky every six months, and nobody can look at more than a billion sources alone. We want the public to do with SPHEREx what volunteers of Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 did with WISE: blink, notice, report. The review queue is the first step: 382 real sources with no SPHEREx examination that we could find, open to anyone. Votes are now shared, each source shows what every visitor said of it, with no name and no account, and a community panel lists the latest votes. Next, we want to moderate the votes and turn agreement between visitors into a ranked list for follow-up. After the hackathon we will write up the twelve candidates as a Research Note of the AAS and deposit the table on Zenodo: Paul, who already has an author account, will submit it with Aziz.

The three clearest of the twelve candidates (methane index below 0.30 means a dip):

1. CWISE J235953.52−280957.6 · T7 ± 1 · W2 15.05 (WISE 4.6 µm magnitude) · S/N 12.4 · index 0.03 ± 0.05

2. CWISE J043050.49−072453.9 · T7 ± 1 · W2 15.52 · S/N 10.3 · index 0.09 ± 0.07

3. CWISE J111646.88−233305.8 · T7 ± 1 · W2 15.34 · S/N 10.1 · index 0.05 ± 0.07

The full ranked table of twelve, with the images at 4 µm and in the methane band, is in the repository.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

- Web tool: TypeScript, React, Vite and three.js (WebGL). Static hosting on Vercel.

- Source code: https://github.com/Paulhb7/blinking-sky

- Data preparation: Python with astropy and numpy.

- Data: SPHEREx level-2 images from NASA/IPAC IRSA, CatWISE2020, and the other sources listed below.

- Hardware: two laptops.

How is your project creative?

- Blinking in colour. The blink comparator is a century old and is used on dates. We also blink two wavelengths, which turns a spectral feature into something anyone can see: the object vanishes.
- Almost no server. Finding the exposures, reading them, aligning and stacking them, measuring the source and drawing its spectrum all happen in the visitor's browser, on NASA's public files. The only server code counts the votes.
- One map for everything SPHEREx sees, at real distances, from an asteroid 3 au from the Sun to a galaxy 49 million light-years away.
- Crossing data sets. WISE colours and motions help select targets, while SPHEREx adds spectral information. For any position, visitors can compare SPHEREx observations with unWISE and Legacy Surveys images of the same field.

Three scales in one tool

The same gesture, click and blink, works at three scales of the Universe.

- The Solar System. The Sun, the Earth and the planets on their orbits, with 7,083 asteroids and comets seen by SPHEREx. Here the sky changes in hours.- The Milky Way. Our neighbourhood of the galaxy, with the Sun at the origin: 15,739 dwarfs already typed by SPHEREx, the candidates of this work and the 382 unexamined sources. Here the sky changes in months and years.

- The cosmic web. 43,463 galaxies at their measured redshift distance, out to hundreds of millions of light-years, drawing the filaments and voids of the large-scale structure. Here nothing moves, and each galaxy opens on its real SPHEREx image.

The visitor zooms from one scale to the next without leaving the map.

- The sky view. The celestial sphere seen from the Earth, where any typed position opens its live images.

What the challenge asks, and where it is in the tool

1. Enter coordinates: yes. A name, decimal degrees or sexagesimal; any position opens.

2. Images played like a little video: yes. The dates loop, or step one by one.

3. Easy to update: yes. One script rebuilds the index of 1.6 million images; the tool itself does not change.

4. The 102 bands and spectra on the fly: yes. Two colours are blinked, and every band that covers the position goes into a spectrum drawn as the exposures arrive, 0.75–5 µm on request.

5. Add or subtract dates: yes. Same-pass exposures are averaged; a “What changed” frame shows the last date minus the first, with the brightness at each date.

6. Choice of field of view: yes. 2′, 4′ or 8′; wider costs more data, 0.3, 0.5 or 1 MB per exposure.

7. Other telescopes: yes. One click loads unWISE and Legacy Surveys optical images of the same field, aligns them with the SPHEREx image, and lets visitors blink between the three. Links to SIMBAD and VizieR provide additional context.

8. Coordinates in the URL: yes. ?ra=133.795&dec=-7.245 opens the position, &fov=4 widens it, and a “Copy link” button gives the address of what is on screen.

9. Citizen science: yes. Votes on the 382 unchecked sources are shared between visitors, as in Backyard Worlds.

Community votes

Inspired by Backyard Worlds: Planet 9, Blinking Sky asks many eyes to look at the same sources. Each of the 382 unchecked sources can be opened by anyone: the visitor blinks it in two colours, says what the source at the centre does (fades in methane, stays the same, two sources, artefact, nothing there), then sees the tool's own measurement. Votes are shared: one vote per visitor and per source, with no name and no account. A community page shows how many votes have been cast, how many sources have been looked at, the latest votes and the most looked-at sources; each line opens its source. When several visitors agree that a source fades in the methane band, it becomes a candidate worth a telescope's time. The votes were opened on the last day of the event, so the counts are still small; the demo video shows the page with sample votes, labelled as demo data.
